text:
SSDs wear out because of how flash memory stores data. Each cell holds information as electrical charge trapped in a floating gate or charge-trap layer, and writing or erasing that charge forces electrons through a thin insulating oxide. Every program/erase cycle damages the oxide a little. Eventually the cell can't hold charge reliably enough to tell its voltage levels apart. TLC (triple-level cell) flash stores three bits per cell, which requires precise voltages, and it typically survives only about 3,000 cycles.

Drives are built to stretch that budget. With wear leveling, the controller spreads writes across all the blocks so that no single area burns out early while others sit unused, even when the same file is rewritten over and over. Over-provisioning also helps. Manufacturers often reserve about 7% of the raw capacity as spare space the user never sees. The controller uses it to move data during garbage collection, reduce extra writes, and replace worn blocks with fresh ones. With both in place, a typical SSD lasts for years of normal use.
